extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal practitioners, and interested general readers researching justiciability and related limits on judicial power
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic summary of legal criteria and doctrines that determine whether courts (primarily U.S. federal courts, with some UK notes) may adjudicate particular disputes. Covers constitutional (Article III) limits and judge-made prudential rules, plus examples and notable caselaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter jurisdiction (Article III, §2)
rubrics_metrics.description: As an initial question in every case before any federal court, the dispute must fall within the subject-matter jurisdiction of the federal courts as set out in Article III, §2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article III clause describes the types of 'cases' and 'controversies' federal courts may hear; jurisdictional limits are a threshold justiciability constraint (e.g., federal question, diversity, amount in controversy).

rubrics_metrics.name: No advisory opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts may not issue advisory opinions; a dispute must involve a real question of fact or law and must be neither hypothetical, abstract, speculative, nor academic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declaratory relief is permissible when the parties dispute the precise boundaries of rights and obligations (so it's not an advisory opinion). State courts may, unlike federal courts, sometimes give advisory opinions depending on state law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual controversy / adversarial dispute
rubrics_metrics.description: The dispute must involve an actual controversy between the parties before the court; the parties must be seeking different legal outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement prevents hearing collusive or 'friendly' suits. Implicit elements include a party seeking to enforce rights under ordinary legal processes and that the matter be definite and concrete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ripeness (timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A question must be neither unripe nor moot with respect to the timing of the dispute; a dispute is unripe when no concrete injury exists or no concrete injury is imminently pending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unripeness often arises when administrative or other nonjudicial remedies have not been exhausted. Courts look for whether the factual record and harms are sufficiently developed to permit judicial resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mootness (timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dispute is moot when one of the parties has lost its stake in the outcome—for example, the injury has ceased or the cause of the injury has been removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid legal gamesmanship, several exceptions to the mootness doctrine exist (e.g., capable-of-repetition-yet-evading-review, voluntary cessation, class action exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political question doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The dispute must not seek resolution on a political question; political questions are matters constitutionally committed to the legislative or executive branches or otherwise beyond the competency of courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baker v. Carr identified six factors indicative of political questions: (1) textual constitutional commitment of the issue to a coordinate political department; (2) lack of judicially discoverable and manageable standards; (3) impossibility of deciding without an initial policy determination clearly for nonjudicial discretion; (4) impossibility of independent judicial resolution without expressing lack of respect for coordinate branches; (5) an unusual need for unquestioning adherence to a political decision already made; (6) potentiality of embarrassment from multifarious pronouncements by various departments. Examples: whether the nation is 'at war'; whether the Senate properly tried an impeached officer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing (constitutional requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing determines whether the party bringing the suit is an appropriate party to request adjudication of a particular issue; it is a threshold question of whether the party is proper to establish an actual adversarial issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standing requires a party seeking to enforce rights under law, generally reflecting that the dispute concern a definite and concrete matter and adverse legal interests between the parties. The article references leading standing cases (e.g., Flast v. Cohen, Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife) and notes standing can be outcome-determinative even when other justiciability factors are satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional vs. prudential justiciability rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Justiciability rules can be constitutional (stemming from explicit or implicit limits in Article III) or prudential (judge-made rules where courts decline to decide even if constitutional factors are met).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional rules are rooted in the text and structure of the Constitution; prudential rules arise from judicially created doctrines about when it is appropriate to resolve disputes (and Congress can modify prudential rules by statute).

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule against taxpayer standing
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal or state taxpayer standing is generally disallowed as a prudential rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are exceptions rooted in the First Amendment (and certain other narrow contexts). The article cites Flast v. Cohen as a relevant case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule against third‑party standing
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts generally disallow third‑party standing—claimants cannot ordinarily assert the rights of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a prudential limitation, though various exceptions (see representational standing below) allow some forms of third‑party or associational litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule against generalized grievances
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts disfavour suits that raise generalized grievances shared in substantially equal measure by a large class of citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalized grievances typically fail the injury-in-fact requirement for standing and are treated as non-justiciable under prudential rules unless particularized injury can be shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zone of interest test
rubrics_metrics.description: A prudential standing limitation requiring that a plaintiff's asserted interest fall within the 'zone of interests' arguably protected or regulated by the statute or constitutional provision in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to determine whether a plaintiff is the proper party to sue under statutory causes of action and represents a judicially imposed limitation on access to courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representational standing (associational/organizational exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization or association may represent its members and pursue claims on their behalf under representational standing rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other representational forms include agents representing principals, states representing citizens, assignees prosecuting assigned claims, and First Amendment overbreadth contexts where claims involving the rights of potentially chilled third parties may be pursued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal and state legislative standing
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators may have standing to litigate claims that defend their institution's powers and prerogatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a prudential exception allowing certain institutional actors to sue to protect legislative prerogatives; its availability and contours vary by context and court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse intervenor standing
rubrics_metrics.description: An adverse third party may intervene in litigation where the initial adverse parties have reached a tentative agreement that would result in a friendly suit, provided the adverse intervenor will suffer some concrete harm if the outcome stands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows intervention to preserve a genuine adversarial context and prevent circumvention of justiciability limits through settlements that remove concrete adverseness.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-court differences (advisory opinions and ministerial exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: State courts are not bound by Article III and some permit advisory opinions; under the 'ministerial exception' (First Amendment), courts may decline to hear suits that necessarily implicate the truth or falsity of religious doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal decisions on mootness and advisory opinions may be persuasive but are not controlling on state courts. The ministerial exception is a specific non-justiciability rule rooted in religious freedom considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete and definite matter requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For a dispute to be adjudicable it must concern a definite and concrete matter, not an abstract or speculative one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This undergirds multiple justiciability doctrines (standing, ripeness, advisory-opinion prohibition) and is referenced in the text as an implicit requirement for a 'case or controversy.'
